Thomas asked, a flicker of amusement playing in his eyes as he watched her. "Oh, no, not a criticism," she conceded, "just... an observation. You're five years my senior, you've traveled the world, built this impressive engineering firm from nothing, and yet sometimes there's a sort of effortless grace about you that makes me feel positively ancient."

"You imply I'm shallow, don't you?" Thomas said, setting down his cup with a deliberate clink. "You think I'm a fortunate fellow who has never truly struggled, but I assure you it is not so! I just think I am a rather ordinary man who has been granted an exceptional series of chances. I would have made a reasonable living, I believe, in any walk of life, however modest. But as it was, when I was a young man, growing up in that little village, I used to remind myself, 'You imagine success will come easily, but many men of fortune have faced hardship, anything may happen!'"

"But it always did," Eleanor said, with a soft sigh. "Opportunities arrived, doors opened. For me, it has been a constant pushing, a slow, determined climb." "And that, my dear, is why I admire you so profoundly," Thomas said, leaning forward to take her hand, "you are one of those rare souls who create their own luck, who forge their path with sheer will. And you are the truly fortunate one, for you savor every triumph with a special joy that I, perhaps, can only understand through your eyes."

"Oh, Thomas!" she whispered, her eyes shining. He caught her around the waist as she moved closer, and Eleanor laid a tender kiss on his temple. "But do you truly love me, Ella?" Thomas asked, his voice a murmur against her hair. "But I do, with all my heart!" she answered, a soft chuckle escaping her lips. "Why do you always voice such a persistent question? "Except for that brief misunderstanding with Lady Henrietta, as I told you, and after six months she left me for a diplomat with a grand title but absolutely no sense of humor, Eleanor, and had the audacity to send me an invitation to the wedding!" "Thomas, and you went?" "Of course I went!" Thomas declared. "Oh, Thomas!" and Eleanor gave him another kiss, amidst a ripple of laughter, and then stood up to fetch her shawl.

It was a glorious evening, and they were headed towards the old oak grove, where the late moon would cast long shadows. But first they went through the conservatory, in the rich, fading light, to examine the new orchid blooms and to confirm arrangements for the floral displays for the ceremony two weeks hence. "Where are we going, after all?" Eleanor asked idly, her eyes flitting from the delicate petals to the glass ceiling, and the darkening sky beyond. Thomas for answer pressed a small, embossed card into her hand. "Paris!" she breathed; her radiant look flashed suddenly to him. "Oh, Thomas!" And as they walked on, he heard a little sigh of utter contentment beside him. "It's too much!" said Eleanor. "To see Paris--with you!" "Wherever you go, you go with me," he reminded her, with a glance that brought a sudden flush to her cheeks.

And there are some delightful parcels for you, so come up to my sitting room, and we shall unveil them!"

"Aunt Margaret, I am so happy I fear my heart will simply burst!" said Eleanor, ten minutes later, surrounded by silk ribbons and tissue paper. "Well, you ought to be, my dear girl! And then we spoke for what seemed like hours, about books, about philosophy, about life, and I quite forgot all about my earlier weariness, all about the hospital, all about everything save the sound of your voice and the quiet intelligence shining from your face. It was as if I had stumbled upon a hidden spring in a parched land, and I felt myself drawing sustenance from your every word.

Eleanor shifted again, pressing her cheek more firmly against his shoulder. "Oh, Thomas," she murmured, a little catch in her voice. "I remember it too. I had been feeling so out of place, you see, so terribly shy, and wishing I were anywhere but there. I always feel so awkward at those grand affairs, so clumsy and unable to make polite conversation. I felt, for the first time, not merely observed, but seen, truly seen, for who I was, not just for what I was wearing, or for whose daughter I happened to be. You asked me about my father's library, and I found myself quite animatedly describing the scent of old paper and leather, and the way the morning light would fall upon the spines of the books. And I remember thinking, 'He listens, truly listens!' It was a revelation, Thomas, a perfect, absolute revelation."

It was not a sudden infatuation, my dear, no, not that at all, but rather a profound recognition, as if I had known you always, perhaps in another life, and was simply finding my way back to you. Every day since has only served to confirm that first, wonderful intuition. You took my dreams, Thomas, and helped me build them into this reality, into this home, into this life we share. You taught me the quiet strength of patience, the enduring power of careful consideration, the deep satisfaction that comes from building something not only beautiful, but also enduring, something with strong foundations." Indeed, the very unpredictable nature of our coming together, the sheer serendipity of our paths crossing against all odds, only serves to underscore the profound rightness of it all."
